unit_label: CB Module C unit 1: monetary policy (courseware unit 7)

facts.statement: Theory and objectives (courseware): monetary policy is the policy designated to influence changes in the supply of money with the ultimate objective to promote growth with price stability. Money is the liability of the government and the central bank, but an asset in the hands of the public; the public holds an array of financial and physical assets in its portfolio and changes in risk-return profiles lead to portfolio readjustment. The goals generally pursued by central banks: (a) maximum feasible output, (b) high rate of growth, (c) full employment, (d) price stability (or optimal or targeted rate of inflation), (e) greater equality in the distribution of income and wealth, and (f) healthy balance of payments. Instruments, indicators, targets and goals: the sequence is Instruments, Indicators, Targets, Goals; as one moves from instruments to goals the degree of opaqueness in measuring the precise impact increases. Target variables should be close to the goals, rapidly influenced by policy instruments and observable: traditionally money supply, bank credit and interest rates; money supply emerges as a preferred target because it is more easily amenable to policy manipulation and the weight of policy factors in money supply variations is more important than non-policy factors. An indicator should correctly measure the intensity of policy action; the ideal indicator will be influenced only by policy actions; the existing of such an indicator does not exist; among the four indicators of policy (high powered money, money supply, bank credit and interest rates), the first two merit attention; as an indicator, money supply is inferior to high powered money because the money multiplier is a behavioural parameter; high powered money (Reserve Money) is an imperfect but better indicator. Example: variation in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) changes Reserve Money, which through the money multiplier changes money supply, which affects goal variables like prices. Transmission mechanism: the sequence of effects from policy action to final goal; the lag between policy action and the final impact is the lagged impact of policy. Objectives: the principle of n x n objective instrument compatibility (Tinbergen) suggests that if the number of objectives is n there should be at least n instruments. Most central banks pursue price stability and full employment or output maximisation; central banks in some countries such as New Zealand, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, Sweden, Finland and Spain have specifically adopted price stability as the sole objective; encouraged by the success of some central banks, central banks of select EMEs followed with inflation targeting; in the US the objectives are pursued dual (the Fed). Price stability argument: a stable level of prices provides the most conducive environment for investments; developing countries stable prices work better for poorer sections; inflation affects different sections differently and hardships to creditors and beneficial to debtors. Robert Barro, using data for a sample of countries, showed that high inflation (rates over 10 per cent) is inimical to growth and the optimal growth is possible only when inflation rate is below 7 per cent; a recent study showed that the threshold beyond which inflation has a negative impact on growth is lower for industrial countries (1-3 per cent) than for developing countries (7-11 per cent); at present a rate of inflation of 4 per cent (+/- 2 per cent) is reported to be within the comfort zone of the RBI. Reasons for a single inflation target: it is transparent and clear and makes the central bank accountable; the target is rarely stated as a point estimate and is generally given with a band; deviations beyond a certain basis point lead the central bank to consult the government. Intermediate targets of monetary policy: money supply targeting, nominal income targeting and exchange rate targeting are considered candidates for serving as the intermediate targets; ultimate objectives and intermediate targets; central banks increasingly concentrate on ultimate objectives. Reconciling dual objectives: central banks pursue the dual objectives of price stability and output maximisation; it is difficult to quantify the tolerable level of unemployment; in developing economies data on unemployment are weak; central banks prefer to estimate the desired level of output or the likely rate of increase in output; specify the potential level of output; reduce the variability of actual output relative to the potential output (output gap); in developing countries data on capacity level are also weak; the trend level of growth in output could be approximated to the potential output level of the economy; the objective of policy would be to minimise the actual outcomes from this potential output.

Rules versus discretion and the Taylor rule (courseware): Rules are generally preferred to discretionary action by central banks as they serve as: (a) useful tools for influencing the market expectations and establishing credibility, (b) they chart central bank action in specific directions, (c) central banks would have control over the variable/s with reference to which the rules are framed so as to render the rule effective, and (d) rule-based behaviour imparts a degree of transparency to the central bank policy framework. Friedman rule: the important policy rule attributed to Milton Friedman says that if money supply growth is manipulated to be equal to the rate of growth of output, then the price level will be stable and inflation rate will be zero; this is the monetarist school of thought; Friedman guess was that if the approximate money supply growth was of the order of 4 per cent a year, it could accommodate a 3 per cent growth of real output per year and a 1 per cent decline in income (velocity of money). Criticism: central banks cannot directly influence money supply; relation between money and prices could lead to uncertainty in the wake of payments technology. Taylor rule, advocated by John B Taylor, is a monetary policy rule that stipulates how much the central bank would or should change the nominal interest rate in response to divergences of actual inflation rates from target inflation rates and of actual Gross Domestic Product (GDP) from potential GDP. The rule can be written as R = r* + p + a(y - y*) - 1 + b(p - p*), where R is the target short-term interest rate (e.g., the federal funds rate in the US), r* is the equilibrium real interest rate, p is rate of inflation as measured by the GDP deflator, p* is the target rate of inflation, y* is the potential output and a and b are the policy parameters that describe the response of the policy rate to deviations of output and inflation respectively from their potential and target rates. The rule is intended to foster price stability and full employment systematically by increasing the credibility of future actions. According to the rule, both a and b should be positive (as a rough rule of thumb, Taylor proposed setting a = b = 0.5); the rule recommends a relatively high interest rate when inflation is above its target or when output is above its full-employment level, in order to reduce inflationary pressure. It recommends a relatively low interest rate in the opposite situation to stimulate output. By specifying b greater than 0, the Taylor rule says that an increase in inflation by one percentage point should prompt the central bank to raise the nominal interest rate by more than one percentage point (specifically by 1 plus b); since the real interest rate is approximately the nominal interest rate minus inflation; this idea that the real interest rate should be raised when inflation increases (requiring the nominal interest rate to increase more than inflation does) has sometimes been called the Taylor principle. Taylor explained the rule in simple terms using three variables: inflation rate, GDP growth and interest rate. If inflation were to rise by 1 per cent the proper response would be to raise the interest rate by 1.5 per cent (Taylor explains that it does not have to be exactly 1.5 per cent but being larger than 1 per cent is essential). If GDP falls by 1 per cent relative to its growth path then the proper response is to cut the interest rate by 0.5 per cent. The Taylor rule has not been adopted formally by any central bank, however, most central banks are aware of it; some limitations: it is not valid in open economies where exchange rate could have significant effects on the economy; some argue it is not applicable in EMEs in view of statistical difficulties in estimating the equilibrium real interest rate, potential output and the politically unfeasible determination of the target inflation. The case for rules: rules make monetary policy less discretionary; if central banks enjoy discretion, then this may induce them to follow an accommodative policy with inflationary consequences in the short run; this is known as the time inconsistent or the dynamic inconsistency problem; the public evaluates the degree of commitment by the central bank to maintaining price stability; expectations about inflation are shaped by the degree of confidence the public holds in the central bank ability to contain inflation. The case for discretion: continuous changes in the economy and the central bank needs to update its data base to evaluate the impact of its intended policy actions; there will be constant inflow of data and information; policy actions may not be feasible with rule based monetary policy since they are based on guesstimates; arguments for discretion also rest on: (a) uncertainties about the impact of policy measures, (b) uncertainty about lag structure in monetary policy transmission channels, (c) global economic shocks impacting the economy, (d) issues of capital mobility, (e) domestic financial sector fragility and (f) the adoption of financial stability as an additional objective of monetary policy; for financial stability central banks may have to resort to discretion. The courseware concludes that the appropriate stance on rules vs discretion is dependent on the intention of the central bank policy action: in resolving specific issues like financial crises, discretion may be needed; rules are useful in specific circumstances when the central bank needs to uphold credibility.

Indicators and instruments of policy (courseware): central banks monitor macroeconomic indicators such as monetary aggregates (narrow, broad money and reserve money), growth in bank credit to private sector, industrial sales, imports, private consumption, fiscal position, foreign borrowings, changes in consumer prices and exchange rates, and micro-level indicators like the financial strength of banks (non-performing assets) and data on payments. The instruments of policy available: 1. Bank Rate; 2. Open Market Operations; 3. Reserve Requirements; 4. Selective Credit Controls. Bank Rate: the rate at which commercial banks can borrow or rediscount from the central bank; the higher the Bank Rate, the costlier would be the access to the central bank money; in general central banks lend on a collateral basis (whose market value does not change significantly from the nominal value of the loan) and do not lend on a clean basis; in most cases there will be a stipulated margin for lending: margins that take care of probable loss of the market value during the tenor of the loan; many central banks do not allow access on an automatic basis; some central banks such as India, in order to sub-serve certain developmental goals provide refinance. Open market operations (OMOs): the Bank Rate as an instrument is mostly indicative in the sense it broadly reflects the cost of funds in the medium-term; it tends to be more effective if it is complemented by open market operations; OMOs mean the buy and sell of securities in the market by the central bank; the central banks could operate in the primary or secondary markets; operations in the secondary market are much more important than those in the primary market. Open market purchase of Government securities by the central bank increases High Powered Money; and every open market purchase of government securities by the Central bank will increase Reserve Money; open market sale reduces it; the multiplier takes over the supply of money in a standard way. In India, since the Reserve Bank has the captive market of government bond market and the RBI monopoly position, these effects are rather small. Repurchase (repo) operations: short form for repurchase agreement; the central bank sells short-term government securities in the market on condition that the instruments will be repurchased after a given date, say a day, or after 3 days, or after 14 days; when it sells securities, it withdraws liquidity from the market and as and when it repurchases it injects liquidity into the system. Treasury Bills of different maturities (7, 14, 28, 91, 182 and 364 days) are ideal for influencing the market liquidity. Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF): the LAF refers to the Reserve Bank operations through which it injects/absorbs liquidity into/from the banking system; it consists of overnight as well as term repo/reverse repo (fixed as well as variable rates), SDF and MSF; apart from LAF, instruments of liquidity management include outright open market operations (OMOs), forex swaps and market stabilisation scheme (MSS). LAF corridor: the LAF corridor has the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate as its upper bound (ceiling) and the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate as the lower bound (floor), with the policy repo rate in the middle of the corridor. Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) Rate: the rate at which the Reserve Bank accepts uncollateralised deposits, on an overnight basis, from all LAF participants; SDF is placed at 25 basis points below the policy repo rate; with the introduction of SDF in April 2022 the SDF rate replaced the fixed reverse repo rate as the floor of the LAF corridor. Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) Rate: the penal rate at which banks can borrow, on an overnight basis, from the Reserve Bank by dipping into their Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) portfolio up to a predefined limit (2 per cent); the MSF is placed at 25 basis points above the policy repo rate. Main liquidity management tool: a 14-day term repo/reverse repo auction operation conducted at a variable rate to coincide with the cash reserve ratio (CRR) maintenance cycle. Reverse repo rate: the interest rate at which the Reserve Bank absorbs liquidity from banks against the collateral of eligible government securities under the LAF; following the introduction of SDF, the fixed rate reverse repo operations will be at the discretion of the RBI. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority made OMO a viable fine-tuning instrument; in India LAF was introduced in 2000 as a liquidity adjustment facility and to serve as an effective instrument of interest rate transmission. Cash Reserve Ratio: banks by statute are required to maintain two types of reserves with the central bank: the primary reserve requirement in terms of which the amount of cash to be held with the central bank is stipulated, and the other, the secondary reserve requirement in the form of the banks holding of government and other specified securities; the former is known as the variable cash reserve ratio (CRR) and is expressed as a percentage of total liabilities; an increase in CRR would reduce the ability of commercial banks to create and generate loan; in some countries like the US, it is specified in relation to demand or sight deposits. Total reserves of the banking system constitute: cash in hand with banks plus deposits with the central bank; they can also be classified as (a) required reserves and (b) excess reserves; banks hold excess reserves to meet their currency needs (net withdrawal of currency by their depositors) as well as for clearing drains (net loss of cash due to the cross-clearing of cheques among banks). In India the CRR is calculated on average daily basis over a fortnight (formerly on a weekly basis); in terms of the legal enactment of 1956, the RBI is empowered to vary the cash reserve ratio of banks from 3 per cent to 15 per cent of the net demand and time liabilities as at the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight (the courseware notes that the amendment of 2005 gave greater operational flexibility by omitting sub-section (1B) of section 42 of the RBI Act and removing the minimum and maximum limits). The CRR is considered as penal action since the cash reserves impounded by the central bank are generally not remunerated sufficiently; the RBI does not pay interest on CRR balances (effective from the fortnight beginning March 31, 2007). In case of default in maintenance of CRR requirement on a daily basis which is currently 95 per cent of the total CRR requirement, penal interest will be recovered for that day at the rate of 3 per cent per annum above the Bank Rate on the amount by which the amount actually maintained falls short of the prescribed minimum. The CRR stood at 4.50 per cent of NDTL on 17 October 2022. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): the banks hold secondary reserve requirements in the form of government and other specified securities; since investments in government and other approved securities are supposed to be liquid, a rise in this ratio could imply a corresponding fall in the amounts that banks could lend; some banks may maintain such liquid securities in amounts that are larger than statutorily specified mainly to permit them to use the excess reserves above the statutory minimum to augment funds for lending purposes. A major shortcoming of the use of this instrument rests on the nature of the relationship between the banks and the government: governments could induce central banks to use this instrument for supporting their budget deficits. Box 7.1 (SLR as an instrument of monetary policy): commercial banks in India have been subjected to two types of reserve requirements, namely, the cash reserve ratio and the statutory liquidity ratio; CRR is required to be maintained under Section 42 of the RBI Act 1934; the requirement of SLR is stipulated under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949; under the BR Act banking companies are required to hold a minimum stipulated proportion of their demand and time liabilities in government securities and unencumbered Government and other approved securities, balances with the Reserve Bank, current account balances with other banks, money at call and short notice, gold; the primary objective of the SLR stipulation is to ensure that banks hold sufficient liquid assets to meet unexpected drain in liquidity during their banking operations; the average SLR (ratio of liquid assets to deposits) declined during the 1960s; the BR Act was amended in 1962 raising the minimum SLR from 20 per cent to 25 per cent of NDTL; the SLR was raised gradually from 25 per cent in 1970 to 38.5 per cent in 1990; the amendment of the BR Act in 1983 empowered the Reserve Bank to raise the SLR of banks up to 40 per cent of NDTL; after the Committee on Banking Sector Reforms the emphasis of SLR as a prudential instrument rather than as an instrument for accommodating fiscal deficit led to scaling down of the SLR to the statutory minimum of 25 per cent in October 1997; since then there has been a gradual reduction in SLR to provide greater leverage for banks in managing their portfolio; with effect from June 24, 2017, SLR was brought down to 20 per cent; as on October 17, 2022, CRR stands at 4.50 per cent and SLR stands at 18.0 per cent (courseware). The courseware also states that with effect from December 18, 2010 SLR was stipulated at 24 per cent of NDTL; if any commercial bank fails to maintain the SLR, the RBI will levy a 3 per cent penalty annually over the bank rate; defaulting on the next working day too will lead to a 5 per cent fine. Selective Credit Controls: central banks in EMEs play a major role in credit availability; selective credit controls broadly follow the developmental role of central banks in EMEs; they may be directed at curbing speculative tendencies for containing inflationary pressures; they take the forms: stipulations about the maximum size of exposures of banks to individual borrowers or groups of borrowers, the sectors or activities that would have to be supported by bank lending, about minimum mandated levels of lending to sectors or sections (directed lending); stipulation of margins against inventories of certain commodities or raw materials; raising margins would increase cost of borrowing (and reduce profit margins) and thus dissuade borrowers; the Reserve Bank ensures the implementation of the stipulated priority sector targets by the banks in India.

Transmission mechanisms and channels (courseware): the policy transmission mechanism refers to the mechanism by which monetary policy impulses are transmitted to the real sectors of the economy; the channels were highlighted by the proponents of Quantity Theory of Money and the Keynesians; four heads: (1) the Quantity Theory Mechanism (QTM), (2) the Real Balance Effect, (3) the Interest Rate Mechanism, and (4) the Credit Availability Mechanism. QTM: an increase in money supply would simultaneously push up the demand for goods and services, so that the general purchasing power of money falls; the Cambridge QTM linked transmission; Keynes attack on QTM sounded almost a death knell for it and the associated direct transmission mechanism; Friedman resurrected QTM. Real balance effect: real balances are defined as M/P where M represents money issued by the Government or the central bank (outside money) and P the price level; the effect of a change in M/P is a wealth effect on consumption and savings; if M/P goes up, households are wealthier and will consume more; Patinkin demonstrated the role of price flexibility; the real balance effect arises from changes in M or P. Interest rate mechanism: Keynes demonstrated that money influences commodity market not directly but indirectly through the bond rate of interest; the rate of interest determines the cost of credit and hence investment decisions of entrepreneurs depend on the prevailing bond rate of interest. Credit availability mechanism: emphasises the availability of credit to deficit spenders in addition to its cost; because of the risk of default and relative fixity of the lending rates of banks the negotiated loan market suffers from credit rationing; an easing of availability of credit means financial resource constraint on deficit spending is relaxed and autonomous expenditure goes up with multiplier effect. Transmission channels (BIS): the money aggregates, the interest rate, the exchange rate, the asset prices (or wealth effect), the credit or the balance sheet channel. Money aggregate channel: represented DeltaM to DeltaY_r to DeltaP (change in money supply, in real GDP and in the price level); the Money Aggregate Channel through the money multiplier: reserve money or bank reserves changes bank credit and money supply and price level: DeltaRM or DeltaBR to DeltaMS to DeltaP, and through credit creation DeltaY_r. Interest rate channel: Delta r to Delta I to Delta Y_r to Delta P (lower interest rate raises investment and output and prices with a lag). Exchange rate channel: an interest rate rise attracts capital flows and appreciates the domestic currency, making domestic goods more expensive, reducing net exports and output: r to ex to net exports to Delta Y_r; the effectiveness presumes the international mobility of capital and a flexible exchange rate system; central banks may intervene in the foreign exchange markets to neutralise the appreciation. Wealth effect channel: DeltaMS to Delta P_e to Delta W to Delta C to Delta Y_r (change in money supply, the price of equity shares, wealth, consumption and real GDP); Tobin q: Delta MS to Delta P_e to Delta q to Delta I to Delta Y_r; Tobin q is the market value of firms divided by the replacement cost of capital; if q is high the market price of firms will also be high relative to the cost of replacement of capital and companies issue new equities and get a high price; if q is low firms resist purchasing new equipment. Credit (balance sheet) channel: MP to AD to BC to I to Delta Y_r: monetary policy changes could affect the output through influencing the level of aggregate deposits or bank credit; the central bank may act on the reserve requirements or through open market operations; the balance sheet channel could apply equally well in the case of consumer spending. Evaluation: the choice of channel depends on the stage of economic and financial development; the factors that make the choice difficult in EMEs: (a) lack of clarity in monetary-fiscal interactions, (b) under-development of financial markets coupled with lack of integration among them, (c) lack of interest sensitivity of households/business, (d) high dependence on internal sources of finance rather than on leveraging and out-sourcing, (e) lack of requisite institutional mechanisms to provide robust and reliable information about individual borrowers and markets, (f) possibility of imperfections such as bank credit market imperfections being high, and (g) the policy regimes may not be completely bereft of distortions arising from rate rigidities of allocative devices. Most central banks of developing countries place emphasis on the money supply channel; they use monetary targets set as a single point target or as a range; Germany followed it with positive results; the demand function for money in the US became unstable after 1973 because of financial innovations. In EMEs: the asset prices channel would work where wealth effect operates and stock markets are well developed; the exchange rate channel works best if the economy is opened up fairly well and the role of foreign transactions in GDP is substantially high; the credit channel seems to be attractive since it would function most effectively irrespective of the share of bank financing in total financing of the economy so long as both bank and market financing structures are responsive as much to the current economic conditions as to the expectations of the future working of the economy; the balance sheet or net worth of firms plays a part.

Transparency, lags and the Indian process (courseware): central banks around the globe endeavour to maintain high degree of transparency in all areas of their policy action (Annual Reports, Quarterly and Monthly Reports, Special Reports, speeches); areas lacking transparency include minutes of meetings of governing boards or policy groups, information about the agenda, and the relationship between central banks and governments; following the Asian crisis of 1997, the IMF introduced the Code of Good Conduct and transparency in Monetary and Fiscal Policies; in India the Reserve Bank places internal policy deliberations such as LAF in the public domain for comments. Lags: the inside lag (the time required to recognise the problem: recognition lag, and the time between recognition and action) and the outside lag (execution or implementation lag: the time that elapses between the initiation of policy action and its final impact on the set goals; the major factors are institutional constraints, legal constraints, and the delays in determining the nature and size of action); impact lag could be long and variable, placed around 12 months to 18 months in India; research indicates that in India the execution lags are fairly long; central banks adopt a cautious and gradual approach in implementing their policy actions; for example, if the central bank were to reduce the policy rate by say, 100 basis points, it may implement this policy measure in a phased manner, say, in four phases of 25 basis points each; this type of policy action taken in phased manner is called interest rate smoothing. Process in India: the Reserve Bank has an extensive consultative process: pre-policy consultations with industry associations, bankers and economists, surveys, the Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) on Monetary Policy (reviews macroeconomic and monetary developments and advises the Reserve Bank on the stance of monetary policy; the TAC role is advisory), from October 2005 the Reserve Bank has introduced pre-policy consultation meetings with the IBA, market participants (FIMMDA, FEDAI and PDAI), ASSOCHAM and FIEO, credit rating agencies and other institutions; Resources Management Discussion meetings; the Financial Markets Committee (FMC) holds daily meetings and is chaired by the Deputy Governor/Executive Director; the internal Monetary Policy Strategy Group meets regularly; an inter-departmental Technical Group reviews inflation and GDP growth forecasts; the Governor addresses the press through video conference; the video of the press conference is on the website. Quarterly monetary policy reviews were initiated since 2005-06 in place of bi-annual policy statements; the periodicity of monetary policy statements has been revised effective October 1998. Monetary Policy Committee: the Reserve Bank notified the Reserve Bank of India Monetary Policy Committee and Monetary Policy Process Regulations, 2016 which came into effect from August 01, 2016; meeting schedule announced in advance for the entire fiscal year; meeting notice ordinarily not less than fifteen days; the MPC meets at least four times a year (presently 6 times a year); the MPC resolution published after the conclusion of every meeting; minutes of the MPC meeting published on the 14th day after every meeting of the MPC (resolution, the vote of each member, and short written statements of each member justifying the vote; Section 45ZL of the RBI Act); the Monetary Policy Report published once in every six months (inflation dynamics, projections, the economy, the operating procedure of monetary policy, projection performance). Section 45ZB of the amended RBI Act, 1934 provides for an empowered six-member monetary policy committee to be constituted by the Central Government by notification; the first MPC was constituted on 29 September 2016; the present members: the Governor (Chairperson, ex officio), Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy (Member, ex officio), one officer of the Reserve Bank nominated by the Central Board (Member, ex officio) and three external members appointed by the Central Government who will hold office for four years or until further orders, whichever is earlier; the MPC determines the policy repo rate required to achieve the inflation target; quorum is four members; each member has one vote, and in the event of an equality of votes the Governor has a second or casting vote; each member writes a statement specifying the reasons for voting in favour of, or against the proposed resolution. Net capital inflows in the 2000s: India built up significant foreign exchange reserves; the Reserve Bank absorbed a part of net capital inflows; theoretically absorption creates reserve money; the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) was put in place by the Reserve Bank and the Government of India in 2004 to sterilise the impact of foreign exchange market intervention while limiting the monetary impact of net capital inflows; interest payments on MSS bonds are borne by the government; fiscal costs are higher; an excellent example of fiscal-monetary co-ordination. Recent initiatives: the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (MPFA) was signed between the Government of India and the Reserve Bank on 20 February 2015 and adopted the flexible inflation targeting (FIT); under the MPFA the objective of monetary policy is primarily to maintain price stability while keeping in view the objective of growth; the Reserve Bank was to bring CPI inflation below 6 per cent by January 2016; the target for 2016-17 and all subsequent years was set at 4 per cent with a band of plus or minus 2 per cent; with the amendment to the RBI Act on May 14, 2016, several provisions of MPFA were subsumed in the amended Act; the Central Government, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, has notified the inflation target of 4 per cent with 6.0 per cent and 2.0 per cent as the upper and lower tolerance levels, applicable for the period from August 5, 2016 to March 31, 2021; the Central Government retained the inflation target and the tolerance band for the next five-year period, 1 April 2021 to March 31, 2026 (notified on June 27, 2016 and later). Factors that constitute a failure to achieve the inflation target: (a) the average inflation is more than the upper tolerance level for any three consecutive quarters, or (b) the average inflation is less than the lower tolerance level for any three consecutive quarters; where the Bank fails to meet the inflation target, it shall set out in a report to the Central Government: the reasons for failure, remedial actions proposed to be taken and an estimate of the time-period within which the inflation target shall be achieved. The operating framework of monetary policy aims at aligning the operating target, the weighted average call rate (WACR), with the policy repo rate through proactive liquidity management. The Urjit Patel Committee (Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework, 2014) recommended the framework; the MPC is the culmination of several preceding processes and draws on recommendations of the Fuller Capital Account Convertibility committee (Tarapore, 2006), the Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (Raghuram Rajan, 2009), the Committee on Financial Sector Assessment (Rakesh Mohan, 2009), the FSLRC (Justice B.N. Srikrishna, 2013) and the Urjit Patel Committee (2014).

payload.title: Goals, targets, indicators and the objectives of monetary policy
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Meaning:** monetary policy changes the **supply of money** to promote **growth with price stability**. Money is a **liability for the Government and the central bank** but an **asset for the public**, so policy changes **portfolio choices**.

**Typical goals:** **maximum feasible output**, **high growth**, **full employment**, **price stability**, **fairer distribution** and a **healthy balance of payments**.

**The chain:** **Instruments → Indicators → Targets → Goals**. The further from the instrument, the **harder it is to measure** the effect. **Target variables** should be **close to goals**, **quickly influenced by policy** and **observable**: **money supply, bank credit, interest rates**. **Money supply** is preferred because policy factors dominate it. An **indicator** should show the **intensity of policy**: of the four (**high powered money, money supply, bank credit, interest rates**), **high powered (reserve) money** is the better indicator since the **money multiplier is behavioural**. Example: a **CRR change** alters **reserve money**, then **money supply**, then **prices**.

**Tinbergen principle:** **n objectives need at least n instruments**.

**Price stability argument:** it gives investors a **stable climate**, protects **poorer sections**, and avoids **redistribution between creditors and debtors**. **Barro**: **inflation above about 10 per cent hurts growth**, **optimal growth** needs inflation **below about 7 per cent**; a recent study puts the **threshold at 1-3 per cent for industrial** and **7-11 per cent for developing** countries; the courseware reports that **4 per cent (± 2 per cent)** is the **comfort zone** for the Reserve Bank.

**Single inflation target:** **transparent, clear, holds the bank accountable**; given as a **band**. Some countries (**New Zealand, Canada, UK, Australia, Sweden, Finland, Spain**) adopt **price stability as the sole objective**; the **US** follows a **dual mandate**.

**Reconciling dual objectives:** **unemployment data are weak**, so banks estimate **potential output** and try to **minimise the output gap** (actual vs potential output); in developing economies the **trend growth** is used as a proxy.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Targets and indicators let the central bank steer toward the final goals in stages.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the sequence linking instruments to goals in monetary policy?

payload.title: Rules versus discretion: Friedman rule and the Taylor rule
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why rules:** they **shape expectations and credibility**, **chart a direction**, require **control of the rule variable** and make policy **transparent**.

**Friedman rule:** make **money supply growth equal to output growth** and prices stay stable (inflation zero). **Friedman guess:** about **4 per cent** money growth to allow **3 per cent real growth** and **1 per cent decline in velocity**. **Criticisms:** the bank **cannot directly control money supply** and the money-price link may shift with **payments technology**.

**Taylor rule (John B Taylor):** **R = r* + p + a(y - y*) + b(p - p*)**, where **R** is the **target short-term rate**, **r*** the **equilibrium real rate**, **p** inflation, **p*** target inflation, **y** output and **y*** potential output; **a and b** are **policy weights** (Taylor proposed **a = b = 0.5**).

- A **1 percentage point rise in inflation** calls for a **rise in the nominal rate of more than 1 point** (**1 + b**, so **1.5** with b = 0.5): the **Taylor principle**.
- A **1 per cent fall of GDP below potential** calls for a **0.5 per cent cut**.
- **Limits:** it is **not valid in open economies** with significant exchange rate effects and is **hard to apply in EMEs** (equilibrium real rate, potential output and the target are hard to measure). **No central bank formally adopts it.**

**Case for rules:** discretion can lead to **time inconsistency** (short-run **accommodation** with long-run inflation); **credibility** depends on **commitment**.

**Case for discretion:** **uncertainty** about **policy impact and lags**, **global shocks**, **capital mobility**, **financial sector fragility** and **financial stability** needs. **Conclusion:** **rules** suit routine price stability and **credibility**; **discretion** suits **crises**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Taylor principle requires the real interest rate to rise when inflation rises.

self_check.prompt_text: According to the Taylor rule with b = 0.5, by how much should the nominal rate rise when inflation rises by one percentage point?

payload.title: Instruments: Bank Rate, OMO, LAF, CRR, SLR and selective credit control
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Indicators watched:** **narrow, broad and reserve money**, **bank credit**, **industrial sales**, **imports**, **consumption**, **fiscal position**, **prices**, **exchange rates**, **NPAs and payment data**.

**Instruments:** **Bank Rate**, **Open Market Operations**, **reserve requirements** and **selective credit control**.

- **Bank Rate:** rate at which commercial banks **borrow or rediscount** from the central bank; lending is **collateralised** with **margins**; indicative, effective with OMOs; in India also used for **refinance**.
- **OMOs:** **buy and sell** government securities (mostly **secondary market**). **Purchase raises** high powered money; **sale reduces** it. In India the effect is **small** because the Reserve Bank has a **captive government securities market**. **Repos**: the bank **sells** securities with a promise to **buy back** (withdraws liquidity); **reverse repos** inject liquidity. Treasury bills of **7, 14, 28, 91, 182, 364 days** suit fine-tuning.
- **LAF (introduced 2000):** **overnight and term repo and reverse repo**, the **SDF** and the **MSF**. **Corridor:** **MSF (ceiling)**, **policy repo rate (middle)**, **SDF (floor)**. **SDF**: **uncollateralised** deposits at **25 basis points below repo** (from **April 2022**, replacing the fixed reverse repo as the floor). **MSF**: **penal** borrowing by dipping into **SLR securities up to 2 per cent**, at **25 basis points above repo**. **Main liquidity tool**: **14-day variable rate term repo/reverse repo** timed with the **CRR cycle**.
- **CRR (Section 42, RBI Act):** **primary reserve** held with the central bank as a **percentage of net demand and time liabilities**; averaged over a **fortnight**; the **3 to 15 per cent** limits were **removed by the 2005 amendment**; **no interest** paid (from **fortnight beginning 31 March 2007**); the daily minimum is **95 per cent**; default penal interest **3 per cent per annum above the Bank Rate**. **Banks hold excess reserves** for **currency drain and clearing drain**.
- **SLR (Section 24, BR Act):** **secondary reserve** in **government and approved securities, balances, gold and call money**; **history:** **20 to 25 per cent (1962)**, **25 to 38.5 per cent (1970-1990)**, **up to 40 per cent power (1983)**, **scaled down to 25 per cent (October 1997)**, **20 per cent (June 2017)**; the **courseware shortcoming**: governments can use SLR to **finance deficits** cheaply. **Penalty:** **3 per cent over the bank rate**, **5 per cent** if it continues.
- **Selective credit control:** **exposure limits**, **directed lending (priority sector)**, **higher margins on commodity inventories**; used **sparingly**.

payload.title: Monetary policy transmission mechanisms and channels
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Four traditional mechanisms:** (1) **Quantity theory** (money supply changes shift **prices**; Cambridge version; **Keynes** attacked it; **Friedman** revived it); (2) **Real balance effect** (**M/P**: higher real balances make households **wealthier and consume more**); (3) **Interest rate mechanism** (money affects **bond rates**, then **investment**: Keynes); (4) **Credit availability** (**credit rationing**; easier availability raises **autonomous spending** with a multiplier).

**Channels (BIS):**

| Channel | Chain |
| --- | --- |
| **Money aggregate** | **ΔM → ΔY → ΔP**; via reserves: **ΔRM → ΔMS → ΔP** |
| **Interest rate** | **Δr → ΔI → ΔY → ΔP** |
| **Exchange rate** | **r → exchange rate → net exports → ΔY**; needs **capital mobility** and a **flexible rate** |
| **Wealth / asset price** | **ΔMS → equity prices → wealth → consumption → ΔY**; **Tobin's q** = **market value / replacement cost** (**high q** encourages **investment**) |
| **Credit / balance sheet** | **MP → deposits and bank credit → investment → ΔY**; affects **small firms** and **consumer spending** |

**Evaluation:** the best channel depends on the **stage of development**. **EMEs** face **fiscal-monetary unclarity**, **underdeveloped, poorly integrated markets**, **low interest sensitivity**, **reliance on internal finance**, **weak credit information** and **rate rigidities**. Developing countries stress the **money supply channel** (point or range **monetary targets**, as **Germany** did), but **money demand became unstable** (US after **1973**). In EMEs the **asset price** channel needs **developed stock markets**, the **exchange rate** channel needs an **open economy**, and the **credit** channel is attractive if **bank and market finance** respond to **expectations**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Different economies rely on different channels depending on how developed their markets are.

payload.title: Transparency, lags and the monetary policy process in India
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Transparency:** central banks publish **annual, quarterly and monthly reports**, speeches and data; weaker areas include **minutes**, **agendas** and the **relationship with government**; after the **Asian crisis (1997)** the **IMF** issued a **Code of Good Conduct**; the Reserve Bank puts **LAF-type deliberations** in the **public domain**.

**Lags:** **inside lag** (**recognition** and decision) and **outside lag** (**implementation** and impact: **institutional and legal constraints** and uncertainty about **size and nature of action**); the **impact lag** is about **12 to 18 months** in India. **Interest rate smoothing** means changing the rate in **phased steps** (for example **four steps of 25 basis points** for a 100 point change).

**Indian consultative process:** **pre-policy consultations** with **IBA, FIMMDA, FEDAI, PDAI, ASSOCHAM, FIEO and rating agencies** (from **October 2005**), **Resources Management meetings**, the **Technical Advisory Committee**, the **Financial Markets Committee (daily)**, the **Monetary Policy Strategy Group**, the **Governor's press conference**. **Quarterly reviews** began in **2005-06**.

**Monetary Policy Committee (Sections 45ZB-45ZL, RBI Act):** **six members**: **Governor (Chair, ex officio)**, **Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy**, **one RBI officer** nominated by the Central Board and **three external members** appointed by the Central Government for **four years**. It meets **at least four times a year** (**currently six**); **quorum four**; **one vote each**, the **Governor has a casting vote** on a tie; each member **writes a statement** explaining the vote; the **resolution** is published after each meeting and **minutes on the 14th day**; the **Monetary Policy Report** is published **every six months**.

**Flexible inflation targeting:** the **Monetary Policy Framework Agreement of 20 February 2015** set the goal of **below 6 per cent by January 2016** and **4 per cent ± 2 per cent** thereafter (**upper 6, lower 2**); the **May 2016 amendment** put it into the Act; **failure** means inflation stays **above the upper or below the lower level for three consecutive quarters**, after which the Bank **reports to the Central Government** the **reasons**, **remedial actions** and **time to return**. The **operating target** is the **weighted average call rate** aligned with the **policy repo rate**.

**Capital inflows in the 2000s:** the **Market Stabilisation Scheme (2004)** sterilised inflows, with **interest costs borne by the Government**, a model of **fiscal-monetary co-ordination**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The MPC makes monetary policy a collective, transparent and inflation-targeting decision.
